corpus_definition: To protect things so they are not wasted or destroyed.

forms.definition: the protection of nature, energy or water from waste or damage
forms.example: Water conservation is very important in the dry regions of Uzbekistan.

syn.note: Related: keeping something safe from harm; not only about saving it from waste.
Close, a little formal; often used for old buildings and traditions.
Easy word: 'energy saving' means almost the same as 'energy conservation'.

ant.note: Using more than you need, so it is lost.
Damaging something so badly that it is gone.

forms.definition: to use something carefully so that it is not wasted
forms.example: Turn off the lights to conserve electricity.

syn.note: Everyday word: 'save water' means the same as 'conserve water'.
Keep something in its good, original state, often for the future.
Related: keep something safe from harm or danger.

ant.note: Use too much of something, or use it badly.
Formal: waste money, time or chances in a careless way.

forms.definition: not liking sudden changes or new ideas
forms.example: My grandparents are quite conservative about clothes.
forms.note: Belongs to conserve = keep old ways and traditions, not saving water or energy. Also used in politics.

forms.definition: in a careful, traditional way that avoids risk
forms.example: He always dresses conservatively for work.
forms.note: Goes with conservative (keeping old ways), not with saving water or energy.

people.definition: a person who works to protect nature and wild animals
people.example: A conservationist is studying the snow leopards in the mountains.

context.text: In summer we try to conserve water in our village. The school has a conservation club, and the children turn off taps and plant trees.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: conservative/conservatively belong to the 'keep old ways' meaning, so they are other_meaning; conservation stays existing (saving resources).

corpus_definition: happening all the time without any pause or stop

forms.definition: a number or amount that never changes, used in maths and science
forms.example: In this formula, the letter k is a constant.
forms.note: Belongs to constant = not changing (maths and science), not 'happening all the time'.

forms.definition: the quality of staying the same or staying loyal
forms.example: She admired the constancy of his love.
forms.note: Belongs to constant = not changing, loyal. Formal and not common.
There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: happening all the time, without stopping
forms.example: The baby needs constant care.

syn.note: Without any break at all; constant can also mean happening very often.
Happening again and again, often in an annoying way: continual complaints.
Easy and a little informal: non-stop rain.
Related: seeming to never finish, often used when you are tired of it.

ant.note: Happening only sometimes, not often.
Not happening very often.

forms.definition: all the time, or again and again
forms.example: My little brother is constantly asking questions.

syn.note: Easy everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Easy word; constantly sounds stronger and often shows you are annoyed.
Without any break at all.

ant.note: Only sometimes, not often.
Not often.

context.text: There is constant noise from the road outside our flat in Tashkent. Cars and buses are constantly passing, so I sleep with the window closed.

reviewer_note: Noun 'constant' (maths) and constancy belong to the 'not changing' meaning, so other_meaning; no verb exists.

corpus_definition: To build something large like a house or bridge.

forms.definition: the work or process of building houses, roads or bridges
forms.example: The construction of the new bridge will take two years.
forms.note: 'Under construction' means it is being built now.

syn.note: Easy word for the same process: 'the building of the school'.
Everyday British phrase for the work on a site.

ant.note: Knocking a building down on purpose.
Damaging something so badly that it is gone.

forms.definition: an idea or theory made from many different parts
forms.example: Time is a human construct, my teacher said.
forms.note: Belongs to construct = make an idea or theory, not building a house. Formal; stress on the first syllable: CON-struct.

forms.definition: to build something big, such as a building, road or bridge
forms.example: They will construct a new hospital near the station.

syn.note: Everyday word; construct is more formal.
Informal phrasal verb: put up a building, a fence or a tent.
Very formal, used for tall things like towers and statues.
General word; construct is for big things like buildings.

ant.note: Knock a building down on purpose.
Damage something so badly that it is gone.
Easy phrasal verb: break a building so it falls.

forms.definition: useful and helping to make something better
forms.example: Thank you for your constructive advice on my essay.
forms.note: Belongs to construct = build up ideas or help, not building houses. Common in 'constructive criticism'.

forms.definition: in a useful way that helps to improve something
forms.example: We need to talk constructively about the problem.
forms.note: Goes with constructive (helpful), not with building houses.

people.definition: a person or company that builds things like houses or roads
people.example: The constructor promised to finish the school by September.

context.text: The city plans to construct a new metro line in Tashkent. Construction will start next spring, and the road near our house will be closed for months.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: constructive/constructively mean 'helpful', so they are other_meaning, not forms of building.

corpus_definition: Easily passed from one person to another by touch.

forms.definition: the spreading of a disease when people touch each other
forms.example: Doctors wear gloves to reduce the risk of contagion.

syn.note: Related: a disease caused by germs, or the act of passing it on.
Formal: the passing of a disease from one person to another.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family; use 'spread' or 'pass on' a disease.

forms.definition: easily passed from one person to another, especially by touch
forms.example: Chickenpox is very contagious, so he stayed at home.
forms.note: Also used for feelings that spread: 'Her laugh is contagious.'

syn.note: Very close; infectious diseases can also spread through air or water.
Informal: 'Is it catching?' means can I get it from you.
Formal, used by doctors and scientists.

forms.note: No common adverb; learner dictionaries do not list one for this meaning.

context.text: My sister has the flu, and the doctor says it is contagious. We wash our hands often because contagion spreads quickly in a small flat.

reviewer_note: No -ous affix claimed: removing it leaves 'contagi', not a word. Adverb left as no_form (very rare).

corpus_definition: Related to the current time period.

forms.definition: a person who lived or lives at the same time as another
forms.example: Navoi was a contemporary of the artist Behzod.
forms.note: Belongs to contemporary = from the same time as someone else, not 'modern'.
There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: belonging to the present time; modern
forms.example: The gallery in Tashkent shows contemporary Uzbek art.
forms.note: It can also mean 'from the same time as something else': 'contemporary reports of the war'.

syn.note: Easy word with almost the same meaning; contemporary is more formal, common for art and design.
Happening now; used for news, events and problems.
Of the present time: present-day Samarkand.
Related: new is about something that has only just appeared.

ant.note: Following old ways and customs.
From an older time and no longer modern.
Used for art and music from an older, respected period.

forms.note: No common adverb in learner dictionaries.

context.text: My cousin studies contemporary design at university. She likes modern buildings more than old ones, but she also loves the blue tiles of Samarkand.

reviewer_note: The noun 'a contemporary' (person of the same time) is a different meaning, so other_meaning; only one existing form.

corpus_definition: Showing that something is the complete opposite of what was said.

forms.definition: the complete opposite of what was said or believed
forms.example: The evidence proved the contrary of his story.
forms.note: Most common in fixed phrases: 'on the contrary', 'to the contrary'.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
The other way round: 'The reverse is true.'

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: completely different or opposite
forms.example: Contrary to what people think, the desert gets very cold at night.
forms.note: Common in 'contrary to + noun'. A different meaning, 'liking to disagree', is said /kənˈtreəri/.

syn.note: Easy word with the same meaning.
Used for views or groups that are against each other.
Used when two facts or reports cannot both be true.
Much weaker: not the same, but not fully opposite.

ant.note: Almost the same.
Agreeing with something else; not different.

forms.note: No common adverb; use the phrase 'on the contrary'.

context.text: My brother said the test would be easy. On the contrary, it was the hardest exam of the year. Contrary to his advice, I will study more next time.

reviewer_note: Corpus example is the noun ('the contrary'), so noun is base; the adjective is a conversion in the same meaning.

corpus_definition: A lot of public disagreement about a topic.

forms.definition: a lot of public argument about something that many people feel strongly about
forms.example: The new law caused a lot of controversy.
forms.note: Two stresses are used: CON-tro-ver-sy (US and UK) or con-TRO-ver-sy (UK).

syn.note: Easy word; controversy is bigger and public.
A serious disagreement, often between two sides.
Related: a discussion of different opinions, often calmer.
Related: an angry talk, often between a few people.

ant.note: When people have the same opinion.
Formal: when almost everyone agrees.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: causing a lot of public argument and strong opinions
forms.example: The decision to close the old market was very controversial.

syn.note: Not agreed on by everyone.
Making people separate into groups that disagree.
Related: not certain, so people can argue about it.

ant.note: Not causing any argument; everyone accepts it.
Believed or agreed by most people.

forms.definition: in a way that causes public argument
forms.example: Controversially, the club sold its best player.

context.text: The plan to build a car park in the old city caused controversy. It is a controversial idea, because many people want to keep the historic streets.

reviewer_note: uncontroversial placed in ant of controversial (rule 3), not as a form.

corpus_definition: To make someone believe that your idea is correct.

forms.definition: a strong feeling or belief that something is true
forms.example: She spoke with real conviction about her plan.
forms.note: Careful: conviction also means being found guilty in court (from convict).

syn.note: Easy word; conviction is a very strong belief.
Related: the feeling of being completely sure.

ant.note: A feeling of not being sure.

forms.definition: to make someone believe that something is true or right
forms.example: I could not convince him to come with us.
forms.note: Patterns: convince someone (that) + clause; convince someone to do something.

syn.note: Very close; persuade is more common with 'to do': persuade him to come.
Get someone to agree with you or support you.
Informal: talk someone into doing something.
Related: tell someone that something is true so they stop worrying.

ant.note: Formal: persuade someone not to do something.
Informal: persuade someone not to do something.

forms.definition: making you believe that something is true
forms.example: He gave a convincing reason for being late.

syn.note: Good at making people agree or believe.
Easy word: possible to believe.
Related: a strong argument is hard to disagree with.

ant.note: Not making you believe it.
A weak excuse or argument is easy to doubt.

forms.definition: completely sure that something is true
forms.example: I am convinced that she is telling the truth.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Same meaning, a little more formal than sure.

ant.note: Not sure that something is true.
Not sure; thinking it may not be true.

forms.definition: in a way that makes people believe something
forms.example: She argued convincingly for a longer holiday.

syn.note: In a way that makes people agree.
Related: so that it is easy to see or understand.

ant.note: In a way that people do not believe.

context.text: Aziz tried to convince his parents to buy a new laptop. His reasons were convincing, and in the end they were convinced it would help his studies.

reviewer_note: conviction kept as existing (strong belief); note warns about the legal meaning from convict. Negative forms placed in ant.

corpus_definition: To manage to deal with a difficult situation.
particle_note: Not separable: 'cope with stress', never 'cope stress with'. cope with + noun / -ing. 'Cope' can also stand alone: 'I can't cope.'

relations.note: Very close and easy; deal with is also used for simple tasks.
Easy word: 'I can manage' means I can cope.
Deal with a problem or person successfully.
Related: come to the end of a hard time.
Stop trying because something is too hard.
Informal: become so upset that you cannot deal with things.

context.text: In her first year at university in Samarkand, Dilnoza had to cope with a lot of new work. She learned to cope by making a plan for every week.

corpus_definition: The most important or central part of something.

forms.definition: the most important or central part of something
forms.example: This issue lies at the core of our problem.
forms.note: Also the hard middle of an apple, and the centre of the Earth.

syn.note: Easy and common: 'the heart of the problem'.
The middle part. American spelling: center.
Formal: the most basic quality of something.
Related: the place in the centre, but not always the most important.

ant.note: The outer part, far from the centre.
The top or outside layer, not deep inside.

forms.definition: to take out the hard middle part of a fruit
forms.example: Core the apples before you bake them.
forms.note: Belongs to core = the hard middle of an apple or pear, not 'the most important part'.

forms.definition: most important, basic or central
forms.example: Maths and English are core subjects at our school.
forms.note: Only used before a noun: core values, core subjects.

syn.note: Most important or main.
Easy word with almost the same meaning.
Very important: key skills, key subjects.
Related: simple and needed before everything else.

ant.note: Less important than the main thing.
Small and not very important.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Trust is at the core of a good friendship. My grandmother says honesty and kindness are the core values of our family.

reviewer_note: Adjective 'core' (core subjects) is a same-meaning conversion; verb 'core' (an apple) is other_meaning.
